newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Markets seen poised for fresh gains.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Markets seen poised for fresh gains.

text.p: Coffee will re-assess its prospects above $1,600 a tonne after a rollercoaster ride last week in which prices rallied to $1,594 then retreated.

Elsewhere in soft commodities, cocoa traders this week would monitor the degree to which speculators are prepared to cover their shorts after prices managed to escape from the shadow of a rigid downtrend.
Sugar would try to conquer new territory above $300 basis March while the rising premium on the spot contract before its expiry next week would keep the market focused, traders said.

Coffee bulls were unperturbed by last week's price drop, seeing the market fit to challenge $1,648, but prices could be dragged lower during a process of correction if New York came under selling pressure.
"It has more room on the downside," said one, projecting a slide to 136-138 cents a lb in CSCE March arabica before a test of 150.
The latest CFTC Commitment of Traders Report released Friday might provide ammunition for traders desperate for clues on the market's direction.

They would also keep a close watch on news from Colombia, where crops are threatened by heavy rainfall, and from Brazil, where a tug-of-war over the size of the 1997/98 harvest has kept players on full alert.
The latest talking point was an estimate by former USDA analyst Leon Yallouz, which some traders on the New York trading floor put at 24 million tonnes while others had it at 27 million.
Brazilian government and industry estimates ranged between 18 million and 20 million tonnes.
"We will have to wait and see and keep an eye on independent crop reports," said one trader.

The market would also be on guard for a meeting on Thursday in Bali of robusta producers to consider quota allocations following a decision by the Association of Coffee Producer Countries to curtail exports by a further one million bags in first half 1997.
The premium on arabica over London's robusta was expected to widen from last week's closing 73 cents unless New York prices dropped significantly.

May cocoa burst to an encouraging close of 937 stg a tonne on Friday, leaving shorts to reconsider whether current levels represented a good buy-back, although they were some 52 stg above January contract lows.

"I think the downside exposure has been exhausted for the time being. I'm not saying the market won't crawl back a little bit but the general direction of the market will start to trend higher rather than lower," said one analyst.

Cocoa has already absorbed a glut of origin and speculative-type sales, with Ivory Coast believed to have sold some 30,000 tonnes last week alone, and there might be little left for new buyers, paving the way for a price surge.
But contradicting this scenario was persistently weak demand from industry which relies on a reasonably big Ivorian crop and stocks held by one trade house to keep deliveries running smoothly.
"People don't panic until they can feel some visible sign that there is a problem," said the analyst, who predicted a 100-stg rise on concerns of a large deficit this year.
The CFTC report might be seen as bullish as total speculative positions in New York moved to a net short by January 28. Traders would also watch sterling after it weakened last week.

In white sugar, market sources said they would continue to monitor trade buying of the spot March contract before it slipped off the board on February 13 to gauge the level of physical delivery expected.

Delivery against the tape might be the easiest way for the trade to cover previous forward sales, despite the likelihood of more of the lesser quality Polish 60 ICUMSA sugars being tendered, they said.

But with London having resurfaced above $300 after a recent slide to $293.30, the spot white premium would continue to be a focus of interest, especially as sellers were thought to be waiting in the wings at $70 and above.
"If it's all whites-oriented and the raws producers take no notice and continue to sell the market on a scale-up basis, then there is every chance the premium will increase," said one trader.
"And if it does start to increase significantly I would imagine there may be one or two people getting a bit jittery in the short term."
But March/March could still move above $72, after which point Thai millers could decide to remelt raws into whites. --London Newsroom +44-171-542 8072
